title: Silent Drummer
article: Whatever happened to Joe Pagnotta, my wedding band companion? How did his life spin out of control? In and out of drugs, Pagnotta struggled with depression. He was bent on suicide. At one point he was set ablaze after a drug deal went bad. For Pagnotta, the end came violently in a police shootout that might have been avoided. Whatever happened to this good-natured musician who captured for me la dolce vita and all things Italian? This is the story of Joe Pagnotta: life and death of a drummer.
In my mind's eye, Joseph "Joe" Pagnotta lives on as a single, vivid image. He thumps away on his drum kit, eyes clamped shut, his short-sleeved shirt sodden with sweat.

He's doesn't smile, exactly, yet he appears happy. He is far away; transported, even. In this memory, Pagnotta is not a petty drug dealer, nor is he reduced to a horrific newspaper headline. He is a musician, doing what musicians do.

This was 12 years ago, long before his life cart-wheeled out of control. Back then we played together in an Italian wedding band. Friends used to tease me about it sometimes (you're in a what?). But it was tremendous fun.

Somehow, we had a total lock on the wedding receptions at the Leonardo da Vinci Centre. Such occasions were staged by Victoria citizens of Italian descent -- an active community of 5,000. Once or twice a month our band, Voyager, played noisy dance music in its gymnasium-like hall for a couple of hundred people.

We dispensed an unorthodox mix of traditional Italian music and MOR pop hits: Billy Idol, Blue Rodeo and Bryan Adams. I played keyboards. The Italian material was mostly polka-style tunes. I didn't understand any of the lyrics, and when Bill Pecorelli -- our bassist and leader -- called out song titles, I recognized them only phonetically.

The Italian celebrants, young and old, held hands and danced in circles. People laughed and drank. We were excited, happy and the tang of baked meats intermingled with an acrid gymnasium smell: wood and old sweat.

Any lingering romantic notions I harboured about the wedding band disappeared after Feb. 4, 2004. That's the day Pagnotta, our old drummer, died in a police shootout. Police tried to use a Taser stun gun to sideline him. But Pagnotta, clutching a carving knife, lunged forward at four officers anyway. For months, he'd struggled with depression. He'd lost 50 pounds. He was on methadone, recovering from drug addiction. His family says the 52-year-old was so troubled, he wanted to end his life.

'Shooting victim bent on suicide," said one newspaper headline. It wasn't the first time he'd made the papers. In 1995, the headline was "Dealer set ablaze after drug sharing." Pagnotta, a small-time drug peddler who'd gone to jail repeatedly for drug offences, was set on fire in his home after a cocaine sale gone awry. He was doused with gasoline from his child's Mickey Mouse cup, and set aflame with a match. Joe ran screaming out the front door. A neighbour said: "We couldn't tell if it was a body or a Christmas tree."

Just a few months ago, a musician friend had heard a rumour that the West Shore RCMP, alluding to Pagnotta's death, had spoken of "Three-Hole Joe." It was, apparently, a bit of black police humour, referring to the number of shots fired.
Naturally, one wouldn't expect police to confirm such a thing, even if it was true. RCMP Cpl. Gord Bedingfield, one of four officers at the shoot-out, said: "I've never heard that."

This much is certain: Pagnotta's family and friends now question why a mentally disturbed 135-pound man with a knife had to be shot to death. (The question was raised again when 33-year-old Majencio Camaso, armed with a tire iron and crow-bar, was shot and killed by Saanich police on July 11.)
Surely Pagnotta might have been waylaid with a billy-club or a bullet to the leg?

Bedingfield said he cannot comment in any way on the Pagnotta case, pending an ongoing coroner's investigation. He did say: "At the time, police officers felt their lives were threatened. So they took action."

Looking back, that year in the Italian wedding band was among the most pleasurable experiences of my life. To be honest, for me the appeal was an extension of my fascination with all things Italian. My perception of the country was, and perhaps still is, the middle- class North American's romanticized image -- the sort of thing later perpetuated by Frances Mayes' rose-tinted book, Under the Tuscan Sun. You know . . . buono vino, bella famiglia and so on. I wasn't quite like the teenager who idolizes the Italian bike racing team in the movie Breaking Away -- but pretty darned close.

As the keyboard player for Voyager, I imagined myself an honorary Italian. After rehearsals, the band always drove to Romeo's restaurant to drink coffee. Besides Pecorelli and Pagnotta, a few other men of Italian descent met there also. Being in the band, you were automatically part of the gang, no questions asked. There was an easy comradery that I -- no doubt naively envisioning a rustic trattoria or caffe -- imagined was quintessentially European.

Whatever happened to Joe Pagnotta, my wedding band comrade? When we played together, he seemed like a regular guy. Sure, he was a rough-and-ready blue-collar fellow. But Joe was also genial and good- natured.

He rarely missed rehearsals during our year together. He was motivated. Once, when we learned the Blue Rodeo tune, Lost Together, Joe insisted that I replicate the organ solo exactly, instead of trying to fake an approximation. Details like that were important to him.
Perhaps it's guilt that now leads me back to Joe Pagnotta, even though it's too late to help.
The last time I saw him was in 1996, after the burning. He was busking with a guitar outside a liquor store off Hillside Avenue. He called out. We spoke briefly.

Pagnotta seemed different. He looked heavier, and something seemed to have shifted within him. I sensed a spiritual derailment. His eyes had lost their sharpness and focus. Then again, perhaps it was me; my own moral queasiness prejudging the situation. It had been shocking to read the story of his torching. The newspaper carried a front-page photo of the charred circle Joe's body left on the lawn after he collapsed. It made me feel ill. This wasn't the sort of person I associated with.
Soon after seeing him at the liquor store, Pagnotta left a message on my answering machine. Why don't we get together to play music? he asked. I never responded.

Joe's widow, Natasha Pagnotta, still lives in the Phelps Avenue duplex in Langford where he was shot to death. It's an attractive residential area, but her building is the most dilapidated on the block.

The right side of the beige stucco duplex is in better shape. That's because Natasha's neighbour has, with geometrical precision, carefully watered and mowed her side of the lawn. Three panels of a pre-fab fence with lattice-work divide the yard. On the Pagnotta side the grass grows wild. In the driveway, a few feet from where Joe fell bleeding to the ground, is a burgundy Toyota Cressida that no longer runs. As I walked up, a German-shepherd cross with three legs barked at me.

I'd never met Natasha before. She is blue-eyed and terribly thin. When I visited her, she was on a methadone maintenance program. Her face is lined deeply, although she's just 46. She wore bedroom slippers, a T-shirt, sweatpants and a wedding band.

When she was young, she was a beautiful woman. I could see this from a photograph of Natasha taken in the 1980s. She told me she took dance lessons from the age of nine. She'd once dreamed of being a professional ballet dancer.
A framed print of The Last Supper hangs on the wall. The greenish carpet was badly stained. The duplex smelled sour and close.

Nearby, as we talked of Joe's shooting, Natasha's 12-year-old daughter, Marina, sat at a computer. I asked whether it was OK to talk with her daughter in the room. Natasha said it was fine. Then Marina clicked on a tune by the Rolling Stones, Paint It Black -- a bleak rock song about depression. Her mother turned to admonish: "Are you going to play that song?"

This is what happened on the final day of Joe Pagnotta's life. He was scheduled for a one o'clock appointment with his probation officer. But Joe was unwilling to go. Instead, said Natasha, he paced the duplex like "a lion in a cage."
The couple planned to take a 11:15 a.m. bus to the appointment. Joe refused to leave the house. Underneath his clothing, Natasha could see he'd concealed a knife. He patted it continually, anxiously.
"He stood at that bloody window there, staring out the window as if waiting for somebody to come," she said. "I couldn't get nothin' out of him."

At 12:30 p.m. Natasha told her husband that it still wasn't too late. By taking a taxi, they could still make the probation meeting. They were on social assistance, but she had a little money. Joe still said no.

He was chronically depressed. He had grappled with the condition for three years, but it had got worse over the previous 12 months. Joe had given up, spending entire days in bed. Although he'd previously taken a strong interest in their children -- 19-year-old Vincent and Marina -- he now left the parenting to Natasha.
Earlier that day, Joe had repeatedly slashed himself with a knife in the bathroom. There was a rag with blood on it. "He was doing it right in front of me," recalled his widow.
When Natasha announced her intention to call for help, he became angry.
"He'd been saying, 'We are finished...' I began to wonder if he was waitin' for our son to come home from school, because he kept looking at the clock."

On this particular day, Natasha was at home with Marina, who had complained of not feeling well and hadn't gone to school. Her mother thought back to the TV show the family had watched earlier that week, about a man who had killed his family. Joe had shown interest in the program.
Natasha had previously acquired a can of mace. She now located it, and kept it close at hand.
"I put myself between him and her (Marina) with that mace in my mind, just in case. And I had never been scared of Joey. Never. I tell ya, Joey was not that type of man."

About 2:15 p.m., Natasha and her daughter managed to slip out of the duplex and walk to a nearby Mac's convenience store on Millstream Avenue. From a pay phone she called her sister, Rosanna Chartier, who suggested medical help be summoned. As Natasha listened on a separate line, Chartier telephoned a nurse who, in turn, called an ambulance. Somewhere in the process the police were also alerted.
"I said, 'He's suicidal.' I told them he's of no harm to anybody but himself."
As Natasha and her daughter walked back to the duplex, they saw three police cars whiz by. She started to hurry. Seconds later an unmarked police car picked them up.
"And then," she said, "I heard the three shots."
Natasha and her family were driven to the Colwood RCMP station. There they sat for four hours before being told what she already knew: Joseph Pagnotta, her husband of 19 years, was dead.

She believes he was intent on "death by cop" -- a rare scenario that any police officer fears and loathes. Nonetheless, Natasha insists a psychologist should have been rushed to the scene to talk her husband down, just as one might persuade a man on the ledge of a building not to end his life.
"I think they could have handled it a lot differently. Under the circumstances, they reacted to who he was, not the situation."

She's not the only one who questions the way the situation was handled. Frank Pagnotta, 66, is one of Joe's two older brothers. Originally from Corsenza in southern Italy, he still speaks with a strong Italian accent. Frank believes the killing could have been avoided. Although he's trying hard to forget the tragedy, he often thinks about four police officers pitted against a 5-foot-five man armed with a kitchen knife.
'I can't see that. They shot him three times in the chest to get him down?" (Natasha, who viewed Joe's body in a funeral home, maintains one of the bullets hit him in the right side of the head.)

Voyager bassist Pecorelli is a big, burly man who, as a 12-year- old, immigrated with his family to Canada from San Giovanni, not far from Corsenza. He's married to Joe's first cousin. He shares Frank's doubts.
"I just don't buy it," he said. "What danger did this man pose?"
Did police come down too hard on Pagnotta, killing when they might have just wounded him? An expert on police shootings says sidelining such a person is not as easy as it appears.

Criminologist Rich Parent is a 24-year veteran of the Delta police force. He's completing a PhD on the subject of police shootings, and has examined 700 shootings in Canada and the U.S. His 1996 master's thesis was the first published academic paper on the phenomenon known as "suicide by cop," and has been cited by such publications as The New York Times and the Washington Post.

Parent said -- despite what movies and TV shows tell us -- it's incredibly difficult to disable someone during an altercation by shooting him in the hand or leg. Even in ideal target-shooting conditions, shifting a pistol a quarter-of-an-inch can mean missing by a couple of feet.

"If you add a little bit of stress in there (a police officer) might die," he said. "The odds of hitting a person in the kneecap or the hand, you probably have a better chance of winning a lottery ticket than doing that."
Far from being trigger-happy, Parent's research suggests police officers widely believe taking a life is "one of the worst things that can happen" in their careers.

He said police in British Columbia shoot and kill two or three people a year on average. Increasingly in such circumstances, the victims have attacked police (as opposed to dying during an escape attempt). Typically, the victims are mentally ill, often depressed and made irrational by drug or alcohol use. Often, the person has attempted suicide in the past.

Pagnotta fits the profile, with his history of drug use and depression. And his widow says he attempted -- or threatened -- to kill himself on two previous occasions. It happened each time one of their children was born. In one case he threatened to jump off a B.C. ferry to the Lower Mainland.
Parent says the stigma of suicide is, in the mind of the suicide- by-cop victim, somehow alleviated by using police to kill themselves.

"Today, if you commit suicide you're considered a loser. It's a 'boring' event. It's not a big deal. You're a sad, sick person and that's why you committed suicide. But if you get the cops to kill you, you go out in a blaze of glory."

Joe lived a life of mostly low-level drug dealing -- typically selling 3.5 gram bags of cocaine -- and narcotics abuse. Frank and a third brother, John, both of Victoria, have led quite different lives. Both are upstanding citizens. John had just retired after working for Safeway for 45 years. Frank worked at Revelstoke for 38 years as superintendent and purchasing agent. He now works part time at Slegg Lumber, hoping to retire soon in the face of declining health.

He maintains Joe grew up in a supportive family with a doting Italian mother. For some stretches of time, Joe managed to live a crime-free life. He once worked alongside brother Frank at Revelstoke for four years, proving himself a dependable labourer until he was laid off in 1982. "Then he went back to hell again."
It was rock music, Frank insists, that was his little brother's undoing.
"When he started playing in a band, I think he started meeting some of the wrong people. He just went his own way, and never much listened to people, what they had to say."
Did an association with Victoria's rock scene somehow contribute to Joseph Pagnotta's tragic end?

John Fisher is a well-known Victoria guitarist who spoke at Pagnotta's memorial service at St. John's Heritage Church. He makes a living operating programs for adults with mental handicaps. Fisher met Joe in 1966, when Pagnotta was jamming with a band in a store- front on the corner of Quadra and Pembroke. The group played British invasion rock: the Yardbirds and the Rolling Stones. He recalls being impressed because Joe was a "tight" drummer -- sharp and on the beat.
Fisher said Joe had drug problems most of his adult life, starting in the 1970s. He recalls once visiting a house where Joe was playing with other musicians. "It was all about junk, heroin," he said.
Drug habits weren't uncommon amongst the rockers Fisher knew at the time. "People went from delightful dope to using speed to using junk," he said. Cocaine use blossomed in the 1980s.
"Coke is still definitely out there. I can name you lots of people, they're maintaining a habit. They pretty much live for it."

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, Victoria's small rock music community was like that of any North American city, was influenced by the notion that hard drug use was cool. In 1972 the Rolling Stones -- much admired as outlaw musicians -- had released their dark masterpiece, Exile on Main Street, from a drug-fuelled haze. And hip music lovers were already well versed in narcotics chic thanks to bands like the Velvet Underground, whose 1967 track, Heroin, made the drug seem instantly dangerous and fashionable.

Said Fisher: "There was some glamour attached to the outlaw lifestyle, and these were the guys Joe hung out with by the end of the '60s, when he was a teenager ... guys who were only a year or two older ... There was an underground, outlaw lifestyle."

When I played in the Italian wedding band, no one mentioned that Joe had served jail time for drug offences or had been a user. We'd met during a decade in which he remained largely drug-free, said Natasha.
"I think that's when he was happiest," she said.

Pecorelli also maintains Joe didn't do drugs when we played together. Even during the years he was using, he dared not show up under the influence around Pecorelli, a successful Victoria builder with no tolerance for substance abuse.

"Joe always looked up to me because I was always the big leader, whether it was in construction or the houses or the cars. I always treated him nice. When he worked for me, we'd always go to Romeo's for lunch. He felt like somebody when he was with me."

Pecorelli repeatedly lectured Joe on his lifestyle. His cousin- in-law replied that it was difficult to escape a never-ending cycle of getting clean, falling into depression and relapsing into drug use.
"He told me that once you're on these types of narcotics, you never get away. There's no turning back."
In the mid-1990s, Victoria singer Joyce Allensen played with Joe in a rock group called Mumbo Jumbo. Although clean at the time, Pagnotta admitted to her he'd previously had a drug problem.
"I remember asking him what's it (heroin) like," she said. "And he got this glazed look in his eyes like it was a long, lost love. He said it was like nothing you've ever experienced.
"He was a guy who had big-time drug problems and had to support his habit. But he was also a guy who loved his wife and kids."

No one pretends he was an angel. Natasha -- although not always certain of dates and other details -- reeled off a partial list of Joe's convictions. Two weeks before the fatal shooting, he was released after serving 20 days in prison for uttering threats to a sheriff outside the Victoria courthouse. He received psychiatric treatment at a mainland penitentiary, although she can't recall which one.

In 2003, Pagnotta served a two-month term for credit card fraud. In both 2000 and 1996 he received one-year jail terms for possessing drugs for the purpose of trafficking. His earlier conviction was 1972, when he was incarcerated for heroin possession.
His worst offense was committed in the mid-1980s, when he robbed a Petrocan gas station in Colwood, holding an attendant at knife- point. Natasha believes he stole about $50.

At the time, the couple had temporarily separated. Shortly after the robbery, Joe asked to meet with Natasha so they could talk out their differences. He roared up in a high-performance Cougar automobile.

Natasha was unaware of the gas station heist two days before. But the police knew all about it. And when the cops showed up, Joe immediately sped away, gunning the engine. It later turned out he'd taken the Cougar from a car lot for a test drive.
"They're chasing us down the highway. He's running red lights, hittin' the horn, like something out of a movie. I'm going, 'Oh my God!' And they're shootin' at us," she said.
"The car ended up totalled. Joey was ramming the cops."
Pagnotta received a six-year sentence, getting out four years later on good behaviour.

Natasha smiled faintly at the recollection. In hindsight, she said, it was sort of amusing. One senses she was attracted to the outlaw side of Pagnotta -- the part of his personality that thumbed his nose at society.

Drugs and crime were just one side of him. Joe was also a dreamer who fantasized about becoming a rock star after seeing the Beatles on television when he was 13. He admired musicians like John Lennon, Eric Clapton and Willie Dixon. He enjoyed playing tennis and going to the beach. He loved joking around with his family.

Although his job history was spotty, Natasha believes her husband was happiest when earning a legit paycheque. Over the years he was a folk-lift operator, a building framer and a labourer. "He was at his best when he was working," she said.

Phelps Avenue neighbours have nothing good to say about the Pagnotta family. Carol Davis runs a daycare across the street from the Pagnotta's duplex. On the afternoon of the shooting, she was babysitting seven children.

She watched in amazement as police moved in, including a female officer yanking a Taser gun out of her holster. Davis ordered her children to get inside the house. She found herself in the unusual position of telling pre-schoolers to watch out for gunfire. One youngster asked what a "stray bullet" was.
A perceived link to the drug trade gave the Pagnottas a bad reputation in the neighbourhood, Davis said. However, she sympathizes with the daughter, Marina.
"We all knew it was seedy stuff going on there. I also feel sorry for the landlord, who's been trying to get rid of them for six years."

No neighbour is more traumatized by the events of Feb. 4, 2004, than Tanja Watson. A mother of two in her mid-30s, she manages a cardiologist's office. Watson lives in the other side of the duplex. She's the one who keeps her grass mowed.
At the time of the shooting, one of her children was visiting England. Her other child, a nine-year-old son, was at home with her.

Police yelled at her to stay indoors as they instructed Pagnotta to drop his knife. She fell to the floor, placing her body over her son to shield him. For a month after the killing, her son was too frightened to sleep in his own bed. Both Watson and her son have received trauma counselling.
"I'd love to move," she said. "But tell me, where can I find half a duplex for under $800 a month?"
Over the years, police repeatedly visited the Pagnotta residence. For example, in 1999, Joe and Natasha appeared in court on weapons charges after a sawed-off shotgun was seized from their home.

Drug customers sometimes banged on Watson's door by mistake at all hours. She once saw Pagnotta, perhaps under the influence, riding a 10-speed bicycle and singing to himself. A pair of sweatpants was tied around his head.
Watson said she "hates" the dead man for the toll he's taken on her family.
She added: "It's been a horrible thing."

Natasha showed me a poem, The Addict, that Joe wrote while living in a half-way house in the mid-1980s. It was later quoted in a documentary film about addiction. He received $100 -- something he was proud of.
In my opiate prison, no bars to be found Chained to desire, pride flung to the ground.

The word "shame" appears twice in The Addict. Friends and family says Pagnotta was especially ashamed by the 1995 fire, which required skin grafts. While he'd been in and out of jail, something about this highly public tragedy -- reported repeatedly and in great detail -- changed him like nothing else.
Perhaps, after the horror of the fire, people shunned him. Perhaps people no longer returned his phone calls. Then again, his friend John Fisher said Pagnotta burned many bridges over the years.
"He had alienated just about everybody," he said.
Before the shooting, Tanja Watson started to build a fence to separate herself and her family from the Pagnottas.
"Now," she said, "the most I can do is finish my fence down the middle and continue my life on the other side."
And on the other side of the fence? Nastasha is applying for jobs as a sales or office clerk. She said Marina, about to enter Grade 8, is coping well with her father's death.
On their side the grass is dried and yellow. And yet, somehow, a vine replete with rich, crimson roses has managed to wind its way against the front wall of the duplex.

After Joe died, I thought once again of the good times we'd had with that Italian band. I tried to remember him as he was back then years ago, playing music with his eyes closed. There was laughter and food and people dancing in circles.
We were part of something.
Who can blame Watson for building her fence? No one. And yet I now wonder: Should I have built my own so quickly?
